prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, cancer, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but they suspect that some of their costs may be out of whack.
prompt.question: Is it true that some of Vitality's costs are out of whack, and if so, what should they do about it?

clarifying_info.a: Vitality has a few competitors in this market who have seen similar growth, but Vitality is the leader in the space; competition is not the focus.
Vitality is the leader in its category and has over 10,000 field sales agents.

clarifying_info.q: How does Vitality sell its products?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality sells all policies through its field sales agents, who are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium, defined as premium from new customers or additional premium (up-sell) from existing policyholders.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other sales incentives besides the base commission?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. In addition to the commission, short-term priorities are communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost categories?
clarifying_info.a: The major costs are sales, G&A (General & Administrative), and advertising.

clarifying_info.q: What is the state of the market?
clarifying_info.a: It is a mature market. Agent turnover is very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Key Results and Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality's key operating metrics and cost line items for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (figures in $000s).
exhibits.data: Accounts converted: 500 / 550 / 605; Total policyholders enrolled: 1,500 / 1,650 / 1,815; Total premium from policyholders: $2,500,000 / $2,750,000 / $3,025,000; G&A costs: $50 / $55 / $58; Sales costs: $250 / $275 / $400; Advertising costs: $25 / $28 / $30; Profit margin: 9.50% / 9.40% / 8.50%

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Sales Process and Contest Mix
exhibits.shows: A diagram of Vitality's sales process showing five leverage points (Acquire new accounts, Gain active policyholders, Keep accounts active, Produce results/Premium, Reactivating dormant account) and the number of agent-focused sales contests targeted at each leverage point for 2008, 2009, and 2010. Hiring new agents is listed but shows N/A for all years.
exhibits.data: 2008 contests by leverage point: Hire new agents N/A, Acquire new accounts 2, Gain active policyholders 4, Keep accounts active 1, Produce results (Premium) 2; 2009 contests: same as 2008 (N/A, 2, 4, 1, 2); 2010 contests: Hire new agents N/A, Acquire new accounts 4, Gain active policyholders 0, Keep accounts active 1, Produce results (Premium) 4

exhibits.title: Snapshot of Sweeps Week Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing weekly premium as a ratio to average weekly premium (2008-2010) for weeks 1-27 (January through June) for years 2008, 2009, and 2010. Two weeks in 2010 are labeled as '2010 Sweeps Week (1)' and '2010 Sweeps Week (2)'.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: ratio to average weekly premium ranging from 0% to 200%; X-axis: weeks 1-27; Sweeps Week (1) in week 4 and Sweeps Week (2) in week 20 show noticeably elevated premium ratios in 2010 compared to 2008 and 2009 baselines; surrounding weeks in 2010 show depressed premium ratios relative to historical averages

framework: Recognize which cost line is growing abnormally relative to revenue (sales costs)
Identify the magnitude and timing of the sales cost increase (2009-2010 jump of ~45% vs. 10% revenue growth)
Assess profitability impact: declining margins from 9.5% to 8.5% confirm costs are not paying off
Investigate root cause of sales cost increase: shift in sales contest mix in 2010
Evaluate effectiveness of new contests: Sweeps Week analysis via Exhibit 3
Develop recommendation to eliminate or redesign the problematic contest(s)

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, which cost line item is out of whack and by how much?
questions.guidance: The candidate should calculate growth rates for each line item. All lines grow roughly 10% year-over-year except sales costs. Sales costs grew 10% from 2008 to 2009 ($250K to $275K), but jumped 45% from 2009 to 2010 ($275K to $400K), while total premium grew only 10%. Profit margin declined from 9.4% to 8.5%, confirming the extra sales spending did not generate proportional revenue. Strong candidates will quickly spot the anomaly but still calculate to confirm.

math.setup: Calculate year-over-year growth rates for sales costs vs. premium growth
steps: Profit margin check 2010: margin fell from 9.4% to 8.5%, a decline of ~90 basis points, while sales costs rose $125K above the 10% trend ($275K × 10% = $27.5K expected increase vs. $125K actual increase; excess = ~$97.5K overspend)
math.answer: Sales costs grew 45% from 2009 to 2010 vs. 10% revenue growth; all other cost lines grew ~5-10%; profit margin declined from 9.4% to 8.5%, confirming sales cost overspend is not generating incremental returns

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, what changed in Vitality's sales contest mix in 2010 compared to 2008 and 2009?
questions.guidance: In 2008 and 2009, the contest mix was identical: 2 contests on new account acquisition, 4 on gaining active policyholders, 1 on keeping accounts active, 2 on producing premium. In 2010, the mix shifted dramatically: new account acquisition contests doubled to 4, gaining active policyholders dropped to 0, and premium-focused contests doubled to 4. The candidate should recognize this shift represents a change in strategic focus toward new customer acquisition and total premium. They should also note that the contest on new accounts may hurt profitability further because acquiring new customers is more expensive than retaining or up-selling existing ones.

questions.prompt: The Sweeps Week contest paid an extra 10% commission on all premium booked in two targeted low-volume weeks. Based on Exhibit 3, was the contest effective?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 3 shows that in Sweeps Week periods (weeks 4 and 20 in 2010), weekly premium spikes well above historical averages. However, the weeks immediately surrounding those spikes show depressed premium relative to historical norms for 2008 and 2009. This pattern strongly suggests agents 'gamed' the system by pulling forward (or pushing back) sales that would have happened anyway into the Sweeps Week window to earn the extra commission. The net premium impact is likely minimal or zero, while Vitality paid out a significant extra commission. The contest also duplicated the main commission structure (both reward total premium), meaning it provided no incremental behavioral nudge toward activities not already incentivized. Interviewees should note agents have authority to influence enrollment timing by up to one week.

math.setup: Assess incremental premium from Sweeps Week vs. cost of the extra commission
steps: If premium was simply shifted rather than created, net new premium = ~$0
Vitality paid an extra 10% commission on all premium booked in those two weeks, which would be a non-trivial dollar outlay if those are historically large-volume spikes
The extra commission cost appears in the $125K excess sales cost identified in Question 1
math.answer: Contest was not effective; it likely caused agents to shift existing sales timing rather than generate new premium, while Vitality incurred significant extra commission expense

brainstorming.prompt: What other risks or strategic implications should Vitality consider as it redesigns its contest structure?

categories.name: Agent behavior & gaming risks
ideas: Agents shifting/pulling forward enrollment timing to game any commission boost
Cherry-picking easy existing clients during contest periods rather than developing new accounts
Contest design that duplicates main commission incentives adds cost without changing behavior

categories.name: Customer economics
ideas: New account acquisition is significantly more costly than retaining or up-selling existing policyholders
Shifting contests away from keeping accounts active (0 contests in 2010) may increase churn
A focus on new accounts without retention support can erode long-term policy value

categories.name: Contest redesign principles
ideas: Contests should target behaviors not already rewarded by the base commission
Focus on activities with measurable incremental value (e.g., reactivating dormant accounts)
Avoid time-compressed incentive windows that encourage gaming
Monitor leading indicators (activity metrics) not just lagging ones (premium)

categories.name: Broader cost management
ideas: Validate that G&A and advertising costs are also well-controlled as the company scales
Assess whether high agent turnover is driving elevated recruiting or training costs within sales
Consider whether a tiered commission structure would be more cost-efficient than contest overlays

recommendation: Eliminate the Sweeps Week contest for 2011, as it drove agents to shift rather than create new premium while incurring significant extra commission expense
Do not automatically reinstate the four contests on gaining active policyholders removed in 2010; evaluate their ROI first before restoring

Treat the increased contests on new account acquisition with caution: if there is a deliberate strategic rationale for acquiring new customers, keep selectively, but monitor margin impact closely given higher acquisition costs
Repurpose Sweeps Week funds toward contests incentivizing activities not covered by the base commission, such as reactivating dormant accounts or improving policy persistency
risks: Removing new-account contests without a replacement strategy could slow customer base growth
High agent turnover means contest changes must be communicated clearly to avoid confusion or morale loss
Without ongoing monitoring of weekly premium patterns, future gaming of contest structures may go undetected
next_steps: Conduct a detailed ROI analysis of each contest type using agent-level data to identify which contests generate incremental premium vs. shifted premium
Redesign the contest calendar to target non-commission-covered behaviors with clear, measurable success criteria
Implement weekly premium tracking dashboards to detect gaming patterns early
Survey or interview top agents to understand which contest structures are most motivating and least gameable
